prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

You asked me once, on our way back from the midmorning trip to the spring: “What do you hate, and who do you love?” And I answered, from behind the eyelashes of my surprise, my blood rushing like the shadow cast by a cloud of starlings: “I hate departure . . . I love the spring and the path to the spring, and I worship the middle hours of morning.” And you laughed . . . and the almond tree blossomed and the thicket grew loud with nightingales. . . . A question now four decades old: I salute that question’s answer; and an answer as old as your departure; I salute that answer’s question . . . And today, it’s preposterous, here we are at a friendly airport by the slimmest of chances, and we meet. Ah, Lord! we meet. And here you are asking—again, it’s absolutely preposterous— I recognized you but you didn’t recognize me. “Is it you?!” But you wouldn’t believe it. And suddenly you burst out and asked: “If you’re really you, What do you hate and who do you love?!” And I answered— my blood fleeing the hall, rushing in me like the shadow cast by a cloud of starlings: “I hate departure, and I love the spring, and the path to the spring, and I worship the middle hours of morning.” And you wept, and flowers bowed their heads, and doves in the silk of their sorrow stumbled.

Once, as we were returning from the late-morning visit to the spring, you asked me: “What do you hate, and who do you love?”  

Startled, I answered through lowered lashes, while my blood surged through me like the moving shade of a flock of starlings: “I hate leaving. I love the spring, and the road that leads to it, and I adore the middle hours of the morning.”  

Then you laughed. The almond tree came into bloom, and the bushes filled with the songs of nightingales.  

That question is now forty years old. I greet the answer it received. And that answer is as old as the day you left; I greet the question it carried.  

And now, absurdly, by the narrowest accident, we are together again in a welcoming airport. We meet—dear God, we meet. And there you are, asking once more, impossibly: I knew you, but you did not know me.  

“Is it really you?!”  

But you could not accept it. Then, all at once, you cried out and asked: “If you are truly yourself, what do you hate, and who do you love?!”  

And I replied, as my blood seemed to rush out of the hall and race inside me like the shadow of a flock of starlings: “I hate leaving, and I love the spring, and the way to the spring, and I adore the middle hours of the morning.”  

Then you cried. The flowers lowered their heads, and the doves, wrapped in the silk of their grief, faltered.

At the time, the speaker replied that they hated departure. What they loved was the spring: not only the season itself, but also the path that led toward it, and the middle hours of the morning, when the day is brightening and full of promise. Their answer captured a longing for renewal, for arrival rather than farewell, and for the quiet beauty of time passing gently.

Forty years later, the speaker unexpectedly encounters the same person in an airport. Time has changed them both, and the meeting is sudden and uncertain. The other person does not recognize the speaker right away, perhaps because so many years have passed, or because age has altered their face and presence.

To test whether the speaker is truly the person they once knew, the other person repeats the old question: what do you hate, and what do you love? The speaker answers exactly as they did decades before: they hate departure, and they love the spring, the road to the spring, and the middle hours of morning.

Hearing this answer brings an immediate emotional reaction. The repeated words bridge the forty-year distance between them, restoring memory and identity in a single moment. Recognition arrives, but it is mixed with sorrow. The encounter reveals not only that they have found each other again, but also how much time has been lost, how much has changed, and how deeply the past still lives within them.

Decades ago, someone asked me a question that seemed simple at the time: “What do you hate, and what do you love?” It was the kind of question one might ask in youth, when the world still feels open enough to be divided into clear loves and clear hatreds. I remember answering without hesitation. I said that I hated departure. I loved the spring, the road that led toward it, and the hour before noon, when the day was already bright but not yet heavy.

Years passed, and life scattered us in different directions. There were separations that felt temporary at first, then slowly became permanent. Letters stopped. Voices faded. Faces changed. The people we had been disappeared into memory, and even memory itself became uncertain, preserving some details with cruel clarity while letting others dissolve. Yet that question remained somewhere inside me, as if it had been placed there for safekeeping.

Then, unexpectedly, in an airport crowded with strangers, I saw the person who had asked it. The meeting was accidental, almost impossible. We stood facing each other after so many years, surrounded by announcements, luggage, departures, and arrivals. Time had altered everything: our appearances, our silences, the distance between what we once knew and what we could say now. Still, beneath the shock of recognition, something old returned.

After a moment, the question was asked again: “What do you hate, and what do you love?”

I might have answered differently. I had lived long enough to know many kinds of hatred and many kinds of love. I had learned that hatred can be mixed with grief, and love with regret. I had known absence, estrangement, the bitterness of misunderstanding, and the helplessness of watching beloved things vanish. But when the question came, my answer was unchanged.

“I hate departure,” I said. “I love the spring, the path to spring, and midmorning.”

The words surprised even me. They had crossed the years intact. Nothing had softened them, and nothing had replaced them. In that moment, I understood that memory is not merely what we recall; it is also what continues to live in us without our permission. Love can survive silence. Attachment can remain even after loss. A person, a season, a road, an hour of the day—each can become a place to which the heart returns, no matter how much time has passed.

The airport around us was full of departures, and perhaps that was why the answer hurt. To hate departure is to hate the wound that time keeps reopening. To love spring is to believe, despite everything, in return. To love the path to spring is to love longing itself—the movement toward warmth, toward renewal, toward something once promised. And to love midmorning is to love a moment suspended between beginning and decline, when the day still seems capable of mercy.

We met again only briefly. Soon one of us would leave, and the other would remain. But the question, and the answer, made the years between us visible. They showed that even when people are separated, even when they become strangers, something can endure with astonishing faithfulness. The heart may change, but it also keeps certain vows. It remembers what it once loved. It remembers what it could never bear to lose.

**You, What, and the Choices Between**

You are the beginning of every question. What you choose, what you believe, and what you do all shape the path ahead. Life is often built from simple moments: a thought, a decision, and an action. Each one may seem small, but together they create meaning.

What matters most is not always easy to see at first. Sometimes you must pause and ask yourself what you truly want, what you value, and what kind of person you hope to become. And in those quiet moments of reflection, you may discover that the answers were already within you.

You have the power to learn, to grow, and to change. What comes next depends on courage, patience, and the willingness to keep moving forward.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose-poem about two former lovers who reunite by chance in an airport after forty years, using the repeated question “What do you hate, and who do you love?” and the answer “I hate departure… I love the spring and the path to the spring.”
counterfactuals.output:
They met where everyone is leaving.

Forty years had passed, and the airport had grown around the idea of goodbye: glass ribs, escalators, the blue pulse of departure boards, gates opening and closing like eyelids over distant cities. He was standing beneath a sign for arrivals, though he had come to send someone away. She was holding a paper cup of coffee gone cold, though she had come home.

At first they looked through each other, the way strangers do, each carrying the weather of a whole life. Then recognition moved between them—slow, incredulous, like dawn finding the outline of a mountain.

Her hair was silver now, and his hands trembled slightly at the luggage strap. But their eyes remembered without permission.

“What do you hate, and who do you love?” she asked, and smiled as if asking for the time.

He laughed once, softly, the sound breaking in the middle. “I hate departure… I love the spring and the path to the spring.”

The old answer. The answer from a courtyard in April, from a village road stippled with rain, from the afternoon when she had asked him that question with wildflowers in her fist and no fear yet of distance. He had answered then as though the world were simple. Departure was a door one could refuse. Spring was a country one could enter hand in hand.

Now the loudspeaker called a flight to another continent. Wheels rattled over polished floors. Children leaned against their mothers’ knees. Lovers kissed quickly, already late.

She sat beside him beneath a row of windows where planes glided in the haze like enormous white birds resigned to obedience. Between them lay forty years: marriages, houses, illnesses, photographs in drawers, the deaths of parents, the names of children neither had met. Neither asked why. Why was too small a word for time.

“What do you hate, and who do you love?” he asked her then, because the question had survived them both.

She closed her eyes. “I hate departure… I love the spring and the path to the spring.”

And for a moment the airport loosened its grip. The announcements softened into rain. The scent of coffee became wet earth. Beyond the glass and steel, beyond passports and gates, there was again a narrow path shining after weather, grass leaning over their shoes, the first green of the year opening everywhere like forgiveness.

They did not touch at first. Their hands rested near each other, two countries separated by a thin bright border. Then her little finger moved, and his answered. Such a small treaty. Such a late beginning.

He wanted to say: I waited.

She wanted to say: I looked for you in every spring.

Instead, they watched a plane lift into the pale afternoon, carrying its cargo of absences into the clouds.

“What do you hate, and who do you love?” she whispered once more, not because she had forgotten, but because some questions are wells, and the heart must return to them to drink.

He turned toward her, his face lit by all that had been lost and all that, impossibly, remained.

“I hate departure… I love the spring and the path to the spring.”

Then her boarding call sounded.

Neither moved.

The airport waited, immense and indifferent, holding them in its bright machinery. Around them, the living river pressed on: passports, embraces, last warnings, final calls. But they sat very still, two former lovers at the edge of another leaving, listening for the buried water beneath the floor, for the first thaw beneath the years, for the path that might yet appear if they rose together and followed it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a nostalgic, Arabic-modernist style monologue in which an aging narrator recalls a question asked on the way back from a spring decades ago, then encounters the same person years later in an airport.
counterfactuals.output:
I remember the question more clearly than I remember the road.

The road has been eaten by houses now, or by the idea of houses. The stones we stumbled over have become thresholds, the dust has risen and settled on other names, and the olive trees that leaned toward us like old women listening for news have either died standing or been cut into winter. But the question remained, suspended in the air of that afternoon, as if it had not been spoken by a girl carrying a copper pitcher from the spring, but by the spring itself.

We were returning at the hour when the sun loosens its grip on the hills. The water in your pitcher trembled with every step, and a small wet crescent darkened the cloth at your hip. You were walking ahead of me, light-footed, though the path was steep. I was carrying nothing but my shyness, which in those days was heavier than water.

You turned suddenly and asked:

“Do you think a person can leave a place and remain in it?”

I laughed, because I was young, and youth answers abysses with laughter. I said something foolish—perhaps that only ghosts remain, or that people return if they wish. You did not laugh. You looked beyond me, toward the village roofs gathered like sleeping animals, toward the minaret, toward the fig tree in the courtyard of your father’s house. Then you turned away, and we continued walking.

For years afterward, that question followed me more faithfully than any friend.

It followed me into cities whose names tasted of iron. It sat beside me in rented rooms, on narrow beds, near windows that opened onto walls. It crossed borders folded inside my passport. It accompanied me when I married a woman who never asked about the spring, and when she left, taking with her the blue cups and the language of morning. It was there when my mother died and I could not return in time to touch her forehead. It was there when the maps changed, when the village became a wound on paper, when the road to the spring was given another name by men who had never heard the water speak in the stones.

I grew old, and the question did not.

At times I thought I understood it. At times I believed the answer was yes: a person leaves his place and remains in it as scent remains in a garment, as a song remains in the throat after silence, as the dead remain in the gestures of their children. Then, in darker years, I believed the answer was no: place is jealous, place does not forgive absence, place replaces you with weeds and strangers and the laughter of boys who do not know your name.

But the question was wiser than both answers.

Then I saw you again.

It was in an airport, of all places—a city without memory, a glass desert where no one belongs and everyone is delayed. The loudspeakers were calling out destinations in a tired female voice. People dragged their small exiles behind them on wheels. Above us, the departure boards flickered like uncertain constellations.

I was sitting near Gate 18, holding a paper cup of coffee that had no relation to coffee, when you passed.

At first I recognized only the movement: that same slight leaning forward, as though walking against a wind no one else could feel. Your hair was white now, gathered beneath a dark scarf. Your face had narrowed, but your eyes—God, your eyes—still carried that afternoon inside them, the road back from the spring, the light on the pitcher, the question no one had answered.

I stood too quickly. My knees betrayed me. The coffee spilled on my sleeve.

You stopped.

For a moment we looked at each other as two survivors might look upon the shore of a country that drowned long ago. I said your name, but softly, afraid that if I pronounced it fully, time would shatter.

You smiled, and in that smile there was no surprise. Perhaps you had known we would meet in such a place: not under the fig tree, not beside the spring, not in the village square, but between two flights, under artificial light, each of us carrying documents to prove we existed.

“You are still here,” you said.

I wanted to answer: Here? Where is here? This hall? This age? This body that has become a slow country? Or that place we left without leaving, that path where you turned and asked me what I have spent my life failing to answer?

Instead I said, “And you?”

You lifted your hand, the way you had once lifted the pitcher to adjust its weight.

“I left,” you said. “So I remained.”

Then they called your flight.

We did not embrace. Perhaps we were afraid of touching the years and finding them real. You placed your hand briefly over mine—dry, warm, astonishing—and walked toward the gate. I watched you disappear into the corridor, among strangers, beneath signs pointing to cities I had never loved.

Afterward, I sat down again.

The coffee had gone cold. The sleeve of my coat was stained. Around me, the airport continued its great machinery of separation: arrivals, departures, last calls, final boarding. But somewhere inside that noise I heard water, clear and hidden, striking stone.

And I understood—not the answer, no. I am too old now to trust answers.

I understood only that some questions are homelands.

We spend our lives traveling through them.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poetic passage about memory, departure, and recognition, featuring almond blossoms, nightingales, starlings, doves, and a refrain about hating departure and loving the middle hours of morning.
counterfactuals.output:
The almond blossoms open like remembered letters,  
white at the edges, trembling with what they cannot say.  
Along the road, the nightingales practice sorrow  
until even the stones seem to understand their song.  

Starlings turn in the high blue air,  
one body made of many departures,  
and doves, soft as forgiveness,  
walk the eaves of the house we once called ours.  

I knew you first by the way the light paused on your face,  
as if recognition were not arrival,  
but something the soul had been repeating  
long before the door was opened.  

I hate departure—  
and I love the middle hours of morning,  
when the world is neither beginning nor ending,  
when almond blossoms fall without regret  
and every wing is still close enough to hear.  

Memory keeps its rooms unlocked:  
a cup cooling on the table,  
your shadow crossing the threshold,  
the sudden cry of a bird that sounds like a name.  

Again the starlings gather, vanish, return.  
Again the doves lift from the roof in pairs.  
Again the nightingales pour their dark honey  
into the bright bowl of the day.  

I hate departure—  
and I love the middle hours of morning,  
that tender interval of staying,  
when even goodbye hesitates,  
and the heart, looking up, recognizes the sky.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dramatic reunion scene in elevated poetic prose: two people meet unexpectedly after forty years, one asks a private question to confirm the other’s identity, and the old answer makes them weep.
counterfactuals.output:
The rain had been falling since dawn with the grave persistence of remembered things. It silvered the high windows of the old station and turned the iron ribs of the roof into the bones of some enormous, patient beast. Beneath that vaulted dark, the travelers moved as shadows move in water—blurred, hurrying, nameless—each carrying a small weather of longing or fatigue.

Elias had come only because the afternoon train was delayed.

That was how fate returned to him: not in thunder, not beneath banners, but in the inconvenience of a postponed departure, in the damp hush between announcements, in the stale breath of coal and coffee and rain-wet wool.

He stood by the clock, older than he believed himself to be, his gloved hand resting on the handle of a battered suitcase. Time had thinned him and silvered him; it had carved its patient initials beside his mouth and beneath his eyes. Yet there remained, in the stillness with which he watched the crowd, some remnant of the boy who had once stood beneath apple trees at dusk and thought the whole world could be held inside a promise.

Then he saw her.

Not at first as one sees a face, but as one hears a note struck from a room long locked. A turn of the head. The lift of a hand to the throat. A certain proud frailty in the shoulders, as though she had carried both grief and grace across a continent and refused to set either down.

She was standing near the departure board, reading the names of cities as if they were the names of the dead.

Elias did not breathe.

Forty years fell from him—not gently, but like a tower collapsing inward. The station dissolved. In its place rose a lane washed gold by evening, a white dress fleeing laughing through tall grass, a ribbon caught on a thorn, a young woman’s face turned toward him beneath a sky lavish with stars.

“Clara,” he whispered.

The name was less a sound than a wound reopening.

Perhaps she heard. Perhaps some invisible cord, stretched thin over four decades, trembled at last. She turned.

Her eyes found his.

For a moment neither moved. The world went on around them with its vulgar momentum: porters shouting, wheels shrieking, rain drumming its endless elegy upon the glass. But between the old man and the old woman a silence opened, vast and holy, and within it stood every year they had lost.

She took one step toward him, then stopped, as though fear had laid a hand upon her arm.

“No,” she said softly.

It was not denial. It was astonishment, pleading with reality not to mock her.

Elias removed his hat. His fingers trembled.

“Clara.”

At the second utterance of her name, her face changed. The careful composure of age—those dignified defenses built from departures, funerals, disappointments—began to break. But she did not yield. Not yet. She searched him with the severity of one who has suffered too much to trust even a miracle.

“Many men,” she said, and her voice was low, weathered velvet, “have known that name.”

“Yes.”

“Many could have heard it.”

“Yes.”

She came nearer. The years had altered her, but not erased her. Beneath the pale hair, beneath the fine lines and the sorrowful beauty time grants to the beloved only after it has stolen youth, he saw the girl she had been—Clara of the orchard, Clara of the riverbank, Clara who had once outrun him laughing and then wept because a bird had struck a window.

She stood before him now, close enough that he could see the rain jeweled on her lashes.

“If you are who you seem,” she said, and her hands clasped one another so tightly the knuckles shone, “answer me one thing.”

His heart, after so many years of moderation, began to beat like a fist against a door.

“Ask.”

She looked away for a moment, toward the black rails shining beyond the platform, toward all the departures that had made and unmade them. When she spoke again, her voice was scarcely more than breath.

“The last night,” she said. “At my father’s gate. I asked what you would bring me when you came back.”

Elias closed his eyes.

The years vanished completely.

He could smell the lilac by the stone wall. He could see the moon caught in her hair, hear the tremor she had tried to hide because he was leaving before dawn and neither of them knew that war, pride, letters miscarried, and the cruelty of families would make of three months an entire lifetime. She had been seventeen, with tears held fiercely in her eyes. He had been nineteen, drunk on courage and terror, and he had put his hands around hers as if by warmth alone he might bind the future.

“What did I say?” Clara asked.

A porter passed close behind them, dragging a cart laden with trunks. Somewhere a whistle cried out, thin and mournful as an animal in the dark.

Elias opened his eyes.

He did not answer quickly. The answer was not a phrase to be recited; it was a relic lifted from an altar. He had carried it through barracks and hospitals, through a marriage of kindness but not fire, through the births of children and the burial of one, through harvests, illnesses, winters, through nights when age lay beside him like a second body. He had carried it when he believed Clara dead. He had carried it when he had wished memory itself would die.

At last he said, with the broken tenderness of the boy still living inside the old man:

“I told you I would bring you the morning in my pockets.”

Clara’s face crumpled.

Elias, as if the words had struck him too, pressed a hand to his mouth.

“And you said,” he continued, though now his voice shook beyond concealment, “‘That will not do. The morning belongs to everyone.’”

A sob rose in her, sudden and helpless.

“And I said—” He could barely speak. “I said, ‘Then I will bring you the first light no one else has seen.’”

She reached for him.

Not elegantly. Not with the restraint age teaches. She reached as the drowning reach for shore, as the exiled reach for the soil of home. Her gloved hands caught the lapels of his coat, and for an instant she simply held him there, staring into his face as though confirming each beloved ruin.

“Elias,” she said.

His name in her mouth after forty years undid him.

He bowed his head, and the tears came—silent, astonished tears, slipping into the white of his beard. Clara wept openly, her forehead falling against his chest. Around them the station roared and rang, indifferent and immense, yet no cathedral had ever held a more sacred ceremony than that small embrace beneath the iron clock.

“I waited,” he said into her hair.

“I wrote,” she answered.

“I never knew.”

“They told me you had chosen another.”

“They told me you had gone north and married.”

“I did go north.”

“I did marry.”

“So did I.”

“I was faithful,” he said, then faltered, ashamed of the uselessness of truth arriving so late. “Not in life. Life went on. But somewhere—”

“I know,” she whispered. “Somewhere, we remained.”

They held one another with all the chastened hunger of those who no longer ask time to be kind, only to pause. Their bodies were old; their grief was young. It stood between them barefoot in the rain, still seventeen, still nineteen, still waiting at a gate under lilac and moon.

The station clock struck four.

Neither turned to look at it.

Outside, beyond the arched windows, the rain began to lighten. A narrow seam of gold opened in the western clouds, and into the gray world there entered, timidly, magnificently, the first light of evening.

Clara lifted her face.

Elias saw it touch her cheek.

For a moment, he thought wildly that he had brought it after all.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a Mahmoud Darwish-like prose poem about lost love and exile, centered on an old question—“What do you hate, and who do you love?”—asked once near a spring and again decades later in an airport.
counterfactuals.output:
Near the spring, when the hills were still learning our names,  
you asked me the old question as if it were a cup of water:

**What do you hate, and who do you love?**

I was young enough to answer quickly.  
I hated the soldier’s boot in the dust,  
the border drawn through a loaf of bread,  
the key that outlived its door,  
the map that made a wound of my mother’s lap.  
And I loved—  
I said your name, perhaps.  
Or I said the almond tree.  
Or I said the country, because you were standing in it  
and the country had your eyes.

The spring went on speaking after we left.  
Water has no passport,  
yet it knows the shape of every stone it loses.

Years passed.  
The village became a rumor the old repeated  
until even the rumor grew old.  
Our house became a photograph,  
then a silence inside the photograph.  
I carried you with me the way exiles carry the sky:  
not above them, but folded in the chest,  
blue and suffocating.

I learned new streets, new words for rain,  
new ways to say I am fine  
while counting the countries between my hand and yours.  
I learned that longing is not a bridge  
but the sound of someone building one, alone, at night.  
I learned that love, when denied an address,  
becomes a homeland no army can occupy  
and no traveler can reach.

Then, decades later, in an airport bright with departures,  
I saw you.

Not as memory sees—  
softly, with forgiving light—  
but as time sees:  
with silver in your hair,  
with the tired grace of someone  
who has survived her own heart.  
Behind you, the screens glittered with cities  
that had never asked our permission to exist.  
Around us, suitcases rolled like small obedient graves.

You smiled, and the years fell between us  
not like a wall, but like rain.

Again you asked, almost laughing, almost weeping:

**What do you hate, and who do you love?**

This time I did not hurry.

I said: I hate the airport because it resembles freedom.  
I hate the gate that opens only to close elsewhere.  
I hate the language of “final call,”  
the tenderness of strangers,  
the officer who stamps the paper  
and never the wound.  
I hate that we became two travelers  
when once we were a single road.

And who do I love?

I love the spring that kept your question alive.  
I love the dust that knew our footsteps before exile renamed them.  
I love the country that lost us  
and the country we invented so we would not be lost.  
I love the young man I was  
because he believed your name could defeat geography.  
I love the woman you became  
because time did not defeat your face.

And you—  
yes, you—  
I loved you then as one loves the first water.  
I love you now as one loves the last horizon:  
without hope of arrival,  
without need of proof.

The loudspeaker called your flight.  
Mine was already boarding.  
Between us stood the world, efficient and forgiven by no one.

You touched my sleeve.  
For a moment, the airport smelled of thyme and wet stone.  
For a moment, the spring returned,  
asking its endless question beneath the noise of engines.

We did not answer again.

We had become the answer:  
what we hated was separation,  
what we loved was everything it could not kill.
